profiles.meeting_scenario: A tertiary university hospital in Germany is reviewing a draft implementation bundle that translates the 2015 DAS short-version guideline into local ICU practice on a 24-bed mixed medical-surgical unit. The bundle already exists in near-final form and includes a one-page bedside workflow, a nurse flowsheet section for RASS/pain/delirium/sleep entries, standard admission and ventilation order-set text in the EHR, and a laminated pocket card for rotating residents. This design review is between the ICU physician leading the guideline rollout and the clinical informatics pharmacist configuring the digital build. The agenda is to judge whether the current package is complete enough for a four-week pilot, identify any gaps between the paper workflow and the EHR implementation, and decide what edits are needed before sign-off. The expected outcome is a conditional approval for pilot release with a short list of final revisions and owners.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hoffmann
members.role: ICU attending and local DAS-guideline implementation lead
members.expertise: Intensive care medicine, sedation and delirium management, interdisciplinary protocol rollout, bedside staff training
members.background: Lena is a senior anesthesiologist-intensivist at a university hospital who chaired the local working group adapting the DAS 2015 recommendations for the mixed ICU and has previously led implementation of sepsis and ventilator-weaning workflows.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to start before the next group of residents rotates in, and she is trying to preserve the guideline's symptom-oriented, clinician-judgment character so physicians and nurses do not perceive the package as a rigid compliance tool.
hidden_assumptions: A package can be pilot-ready if the clinical logic is stable, even when some operational wording and documentation mechanics are still being tuned during the first week of use.

When colleagues say the protocol will apply to the whole ICU, that naturally means the routine adult mixed-ICU population, not edge-case pathways like brief overnight postoperative monitoring beds or patients already managed under dedicated neuro protocols.

The phrase regular delirium screening naturally means once each nursing shift plus whenever the patient's cognition or agitation changes, because that is how bedside teams already think about assessment rhythm.
Daily sedation reassessment belongs inside the team's normal morning-round workflow and should happen when physiology permits, not as a fixed clock-time task detached from clinical context.

members.name: Markus Vogel
members.role: Clinical informatics pharmacist and ICU order-set designer
members.expertise: Medication workflow configuration, ICU documentation logic, EHR order sets, audit-ready implementation of guideline-based care
members.background: Markus is a hospital pharmacist with medical informatics training who maintains ICU medication order sets and nursing task logic across several adult critical care areas and recently standardized sedation-related reporting for internal quality review.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid a pilot that generates rework, inconsistent documentation, or unusable audit data, and he is quietly pushing for enough specificity that analysts, educators, and charge nurses can execute the package without repeatedly returning to physicians for clarification.
hidden_assumptions: Pilot-ready means every recurring task, field, trigger, and exception needed for build and reporting is already explicit enough that the EHR can support it consistently from day one.
If a protocol is described as unit-wide or for all ICU patients, it should default into every adult ICU admission workflow unless exclusions are written directly into the artifacts.

Regular delirium screening should map to a discrete fixed cadence in the system, specifically the existing q8h nursing assessment structure, because reminder logic and completion reports cannot rely on informal shift interpretation.

A daily sedation reassessment requirement is operationally real only if it becomes a visible, trackable step in the EHR, typically attached to sedation orders or daily goals review at a standard time.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the bundle is 'pilot-ready' or 'ready for pilot next month.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the clinical pathway is coherent enough for bedside use and any remaining ambiguity is limited to implementation polish such as exact EHR phrasing or reminder placement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the bundle is detailed enough that build analysts, nurse educators, and reports can all run without needing local interpretation after launch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Pilot readiness is a routine milestone term in design reviews, and each treats their own professional standard as the obvious one; because both want to appear constructive rather than procedural, neither unpacks the threshold explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both endorse 'regular delirium screening' in the workflow and documentation template.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means screening once per nursing shift and additionally whenever there is a meaningful mental-status change, such as new agitation, unexpected somnolence, or a change after sedation reduction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a fixed q8h documented screening cadence tied to the existing structured nursing assessment block, because that is the unit's reportable recurring interval.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Regular is a familiar guideline word that feels precise enough in clinical conversation; shift-based practice and q8h build logic usually coincide closely on this unit, so the divergence hides until staffing patterns, shift timing, or ad hoc reassessments matter.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both describe the bundle as applying to 'the whole unit' or 'all ICU patients.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the standard adult mixed-ICU population, especially ventilated or multi-day patients, while implicitly excluding short-stay elective postoperative overnight cases and patients entering through an established neurocritical-care pathway unless clinicians intentionally use the bundle there.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of every adult patient admitted under the ICU location in the EHR, including one-night postoperative monitoring admissions, unless an explicit exclusion is built into orders or documentation rules.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The unit is commonly spoken about as one operational entity, so saying whole unit sounds ordinary and aligned; the mismatch lives in low-salience edge cases that neither person foregrounds during a high-level review.

misalignment_points.topic: How daily sedation reassessment will be operationalized
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the bundle should include 'daily sedation reassessment' or a 'daily wake-up check.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the bedside team will review sedation depth during morning rounds and reduce or interrupt sedation when clinically appropriate, using hemodynamics, ventilation status, and current goals to decide whether that day's reassessment is active or only documented as deferred.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the phrase implies a standard EHR-mediated workflow step, likely a recurring early-morning task or order-linked prompt that can be completed, deferred, and later counted in pilot reports.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They share the same clinical intention and use standard ICU shorthand, so the conversation never naturally shifts to whether reassessment is primarily a judgment embedded in rounds or a discrete system task with timing and completion logic.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pilot live before the next residents rotate, otherwise we lose momentum and end up teaching two different cohorts. From the clinical side, the package is coherent enough already; any remaining chart wording or reminder placement can be refined during the first week. And when I say the whole unit, I'm thinking of our routine adult mixed-ICU patients, not the odd overnight postop observation case or the neuro pathway that already runs on its own rails.

On the unit, that naturally means once per shift and also when cognition or agitation changes, but I don't need to unpack that because everyone already practices that way.

This belongs in the morning clinical review, with the team deciding whether to lighten, pause, or defer based on stability. turns.inner_thought: That's workable. I can make it a soft prompt rather than a disruptive hard stop, as long as it still produces a discrete status for reporting.
